title: AI literacy and AI governance training by country: the EU, the US, Japan, Australia and the UAE compared
seoTitle: AI literacy training rules by country
description: Where AI literacy training is a legal duty and where it is voluntary: the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, Japan's AI Guidelines, plus Australia and the UAE.
shortAnswer: Only the European Union makes AI literacy a legal obligation for businesses: Article 4 of the EU AI Act requires providers and deployers of AI systems to take measures to support their staff's AI literacy, and it has applied since February 2, 2025. The United States relies on the voluntary NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and Japan on voluntary AI Guidelines for Business. This library documents no binding AI training rule for private employers in Australia or the UAE.
keyTakeaways: The EU AI Act Article 4 is the only binding, economy wide AI literacy duty among the five markets; the Digital Omnibus (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) kept it but removed any guaranteed level of literacy per individual.
The US NIST AI RMF expects AI risk management training for personnel and partners (GOVERN 2.2), but it is voluntary; federal agencies face training duties for AI operators under OMB memo M-25-21.

Japan's AI Guidelines for Business (version 1.2, March 31, 2026) expect role appropriate AI literacy education, but describe themselves as non binding soft law, and the AI Promotion Act has no penalties.
Australia and the UAE have no AI literacy training rule documented in this library; Australia's PSPF Release 2026 lists training on AI use for Commonwealth entities only.
A multinational can treat the EU Article 4 duty as its global floor, then use NIST and Japanese role guidance to shape content, with ISO/IEC 42001 as the certifiable layer.

sections.heading: How does AI literacy and AI governance training compare by market?

blocks.text: The markets range from a binding legal duty in the EU to voluntary frameworks in the United States and Japan, and no documented rule in Australia or the UAE. Because AI regulation is moving quickly, the table reflects the position as at November 2026.

sections.heading: Is AI literacy training legally required anywhere?

blocks.text: Yes, in the EU. Article 4 of the AI Act binds every provider and deployer of an AI system, not only those using high risk AI, and it applies directly in Portugal and every other Member State.

The original Article 4 required measures to ensure, to the best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus on AI, replaced it in July 2026: organizations must take measures to support the development of AI literacy, with no requirement to guarantee a specific level for any individual. National market surveillance authorities supervise and enforce Article 4 from August 2026, with penalties set in national law ([EU AI Act AI literacy](/regulations/eu-ai-act-ai-literacy)). Separately, Article 26(2) requires deployers of high risk AI to assign human oversight to people with the necessary competence, training and authority, applying from December 2, 2027 for Annex III systems after the Omnibus.

sections.heading: How do the US and Japanese frameworks differ from the EU rule?

blocks.text: Both are voluntary and both are more specific about content than the EU rule. They describe what good AI training covers; the EU rule makes some training mandatory but says little about content.

The NIST AI RMF's GOVERN 2.2 states that "The organization's personnel and partners receive AI risk management training to enable them to perform their duties and responsibilities consistent with related policies, procedures, and agreements." The framework describes itself as voluntary, but it gains weight through references: the DOJ lists it as a resource for evaluating compliance programs, and Texas HB 149 gives a defense linked to substantial compliance with the Generative AI Profile ([NIST AI RMF training](/regulations/nist-ai-rmf-ai-risk-training)). For federal agencies, OMB memo M-25-21 requires sufficient and periodic training, assessment and oversight for AI operators.

Japan's AI Guidelines for Business set common guiding principle 8, Education/literacy: provide people engaged in AI with the education to reach AI literacy sufficient for their engagement. The Appendix gives role specific content, from attack methods for developers to bias, accuracy and spotting false information for business users. The Guidelines call themselves soft law without legally binding force, and the AI Promotion Act has no penalty provisions ([Japan AI Guidelines](/regulations/japan-ai-guidelines-for-business-training)).

sections.heading: What do Australia and the UAE require?

blocks.text: This library documents no AI literacy or AI governance training duty for private employers in Australia or the UAE. That is a statement about current coverage, and groups should confirm the local position before assuming none exists.

The one documented Australian reference is in government security: the announcement of the [PSPF Release 2026](/regulations/pspf-security-awareness-training) for Commonwealth entities lists training on AI use among its changes. It does not reach private companies.

sections.heading: What should a multinational standardize and what should it localize?

blocks.text: Standardize on the EU Article 4 duty as a global floor, because it is the only binding rule and it covers ordinary workplace use of general purpose AI. Localize role content, regulatory references and human oversight training for high risk systems.

blocks.text: Groups that want a certifiable layer often add [ISO/IEC 42001](/regulations/iso-iec-42001-competence-and-awareness), whose competence and awareness clauses sit naturally over all five markets; the [ISO/IEC 42001 and NIST AI RMF comparison](/compare/iso-42001-vs-nist-ai-rmf) explains how the two fit together. The [AI literacy](/glossary/ai-literacy) definition and the guide to [building an AI literacy training program](/guides/how-to-build-an-ai-literacy-training-program) cover program design.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models AI literacy as a framework of concepts, roles and assessment points before content is written, so the EU floor and each voluntary framework's role guidance are explicit and traceable. That framework also governs AI assisted content itself, with provenance on every item. See [framework intelligence](/platform/framework-intelligence).

faqs.q: Does the EU AI Act require a certificate for AI literacy?
faqs.a: No. The European Commission says no certificate is needed and that an internal record of training and other initiatives is enough. After the Digital Omnibus, organizations must take measures to support AI literacy but need not guarantee a specific level for any individual.

faqs.q: Does Article 4 apply to companies outside the EU?
faqs.a: It applies to providers of AI systems placed on the EU market or put into service in the EU, including providers established outside the EU, and to deployers established or located in the EU. A non EU group's EU subsidiaries using AI at work are deployers.

faqs.q: Is the NIST AI RMF mandatory for US companies?
faqs.a: No. NIST describes it as voluntary. It becomes expected through customers, regulators and laws that refer to it, such as the DOJ's compliance program guidance and Texas HB 149, which links a defense to substantial compliance with the Generative AI Profile.

faqs.q: Will Japan make AI literacy training mandatory?
faqs.a: Nothing in current Japanese law does. The AI Promotion Act, fully in force from September 1, 2025, has no penalty provisions and does not require businesses to train staff. The Second AI Basic Plan of July 14, 2026 promotes literacy across organizations as policy, not as a legal duty.
